Lecture 7

Original PowerPoint — Lecture 7 (2025)Links to an external site.

590 Lecture 7

What We’ve Covered

  • Week 1: Research Topic & Question
  • Week 2: Method & Recipe for the Literature Review
  • Week 3: Vibe Scholarship - Applying AI to Close & Distant Reading
  • Week 4: Reading Spivak with AI & Writing for Humanities and the Sciences
  • Week 5: Structuring the Literature Review
  • Week 6: Sociology of Knowledge / Reflexivity / Acknowledging AI

This Week - Final Week

  • Topical discussion: The Automatic Academy? The Future of Scholarship
  • Synthesizing the course into a draft review - Preparation for Final Assessment
  • Take summary paragraph from Week 6 and expand into 1,500–2,000 words
  • Re-cap on course purpose

The Automatic Academy? The Future of Scholarship

  • Let’s test ChatGPT group chat…
  • Where is automation happening? Some examples….

Anthropic Interviewer

  • Introducing Anthropic Interviewer  AnthropicLinks to an external site. - Compare with Magee et al. 2023 - tables have turned (AI now interviewing the human)

Thematic Analysis

Human vs LLM thematic analysis: - Algorithms are biased - but run against human bias - Coding fatigue - too many themes, sense of duplication, saturation - The machine doesn’t tire… related but different biases

Literature Gap Analysis - Google Scholar Labs

Sign in - Google AccountsLinks to an external site.

Agent-based Models

  • “Computational sociology” - building models to simulate complex behavior

  • Sign in - Google AccountsLinks to an external site.

  • Claude claude.aiLinks to an external site.

Mathematical / Scientific Research

  • Common approach now to problem-solving - so-called “neuro-symbolic” reasoning
    • LLM + tools - specifically Python
    • Solve some problem - watch AI generate, run & evaluate Python code

Social Science Survey Research

  • Design surveys
  • Generate code and sample data for survey analysis
  • Compare results to the literature

Crisis: LLM-generated knowledge

  • Huge amounts of AI-generated submissions to journals
  • “who, aside from the algorithms themselves, would want to read this LLM-generated content?”

The Problem of Assessment

  • Why do we assess academic performance?
  • Does it make sense in the age of AI? What about Artificial Super Intelligence?
  • Think of the entire apparatus of the education “industry”: rubrics, criteria, marking, validation?
    • What are we even assessing? Individual aptitude, historical priviledge? Or the specific confluence of individual X with AI Y?

Analogy: “High Responders” to Technology

  • Example: Nike’s “supershoes” - some people respond better than others
  • Are some of us “high responders” to AI? Can
    • What is the role of assessment in preparing for a future of work? Is it just an arbitrary ranking?

“Vibe” is perhaps a serious skill…

  • What does Rick Rubin (music producer) actually “know”?
  • In scholarship: developing a “feel” for questions worth asking - and how to answer them
    • Important? AI accelerates locating dead ends… This is not the gap you think it is.

From the Heart of Silicon Valley…

Skills are always “Meta” Skills

  • My bias: develop the liberal arts - these are the “super shoes” / meta skills for an era of LLMs
  • AI literacy = general literacy? The more “expressive” you are, the more you can make a LLM “sing”.
  • Perhaps these skills are not really that assessable
  • What difference does it make? What does a world without differentiation (skills, work ethic, etc) mean?

Implications? The Post-Assessment Age

  • Does everyone just get a free car now? The return of the “planned economy”

Stiegler’s Nightmare

  • The Automatic Society
  • Proletarianization:
    • From loss of ownership (Marx - means to production) to loss of knowledge (more literally “savoir-faire”: know-how)
      • Connected also with the rise of knowledge economy, immaterial labor: work is now cognitive, informatic - susceptible to automation by artificial cognition
    • Plato’s Pharmakon: writing is poison (destroys memory) but also cure (sustains memory)
  • Technology leads to collective loss of knowing-how - Can be “cured” by alternative organizations of technology and social conditions (but how? answers are non-specific, strangely reactionary)

Ruha Benjamin’s Race After Technology

  • “Abolitionist Tools”
  • Translation to scholarly contexts: thinking AI as a liberational technology - non-competitive knowledge without assessment, careerism, quantification, discrimination

Filling gaps vs Producing spaces

  • Perhaps: to re-thinking knowledge beyond a logic of accumulation (the metaphor of filling “gaps” might be a trap for us here - as through knowledge is a container)
    • Instead focus on knowledge as creative, expansive - instead producing gaps, spaces - fractal metaphor

What does this all mean?

  • AI is disruptive, threatening: to what we think of as the correct, established ways of doing things can be accelerated, automated.
  • De-stabilized (already low) confidence in academic institutions - anyone now can produce a report
  • Yet now indispensable to the work of scholarship
  • Requires new fundamental orientations toward the purposes and methods of scholarship, knowing…

Final assignment

  • My emphasis on this course is on the workshop nature of the material - aims to prepare for general / special field, other literature review work
  • Grading will be indicative of this
    • What is an “A”?
    • Roughly 1,500–2,000 words - use of concise language
    • Heavy use of signposting / metadiscourse
    • Demonstration of clear principle of organization (thematic / chronological / developmental etc)
    • Appropriate use of language for the apparent audience
    • Some sense of an independent and critical stance toward your material
    • Statement of gap filled (or space to be produced) by your research
      • And the persuasiveness of this statement, given the preceding evidence from the literature
    • Due acknowledgement of AI
  • I won’t know your field: I won’t be grading on whether you include everything

Activity: Dialectical Exchange

  • Background: What is the dialectic?
    • Socratic dialectic - find the truth via relentless questioning (think: TV lawyers)
      • Truth is “whittled away” from the error that surrounds it
      • Question (Socrates) and answer (respondent) progressively move towards the truth (truth is journey / process)
    • Hegelian dialectic: same idea, but more formal:
      • Thesis: the current status quo
      • Antithesis: an opposing view
      • Synthesis: the reconciliation of thesis and antithesis

Can AI be a dialectical partner / guide?

System Prompts - Claude DocsLinks to an external site.

ERAM 590 - Google DocsLinks to an external site.

Following Claude’s example we are going to develop a fancy multipart prompt: - Assignment (from the syllabus) - Criteria - Assessment - Review Synopsis - Review Structural Principle - Review Audience - Dialectic Prompt

Why so fancy?

Variants on the Dialectic Prompt

I need to write this literature review. Don’t write it for me. Instead, be my dialectical guide. Using criteria, structural principle and audience, help me develop the synopsis into an ‘A’ grade paper!

Be my Socratic dialogue partner.

I want to illustrate for a class the process of the dialectic, with AI as partner / guide. Below is a synposis of a literature review. Let’s call this the “thesis”. Can you examine this thesis, engaging in a dialectical process to pose an antithesis - then help arrive at a synthesis?

Final Literature Review (40%) Throughout the course you will develop a literature review around a research topic and question of your choice. This may relate to a future dissertation topic or question, or some other research question. In total, the Literature Review should be 1,500–2,000 words in length. • Develop novel, significant and feasible research question • Compile relevant map of the field relating to the research question • Choose and apply appropriate citation practices (science / humanities / mix) for question & field • Use framing / signposting / metadiscursive language • Show reflexivity as a scholar • Acknowledge and demonstrate appropriate use of AI • Use all of the above to highlight a plausible gap in the literature - What is an “A”? - Roughly 1,500–2,000 words - use of concise language - Heavy use of signposting / metadiscourse - Demonstration of clear principle of organization (thematic / chronological / developmental etc) - Appropriate use of language for the apparent audience - Some sense of an independent and critical stance toward your material - Statement of gap filled (or space to be produced) by your research - And the persuasiveness of this statement, given the preceding evidence from the literature - Due acknowledgement of AI In this review, I begin by outlining current research on the technical performance and global expansion of LEO satellite networks. I then examine scholarship addressing digital inclusion challenges in underserved regions, highlighting persistent infrastructural and socioeconomic barriers. I further explore studies on technology-enabled learning initiatives, emphasizing what is known—and what remains speculative—about satellite-supported education models. Finally, I demonstrate that while these bodies of research each contribute important insights, none sufficiently integrate technical, social, and pedagogical perspectives to explain how LEO satellites can equitably support learners in remote communities. As a result, this review establishes the need for a unified, implementation-focused framework that bridges technological capability with educational equity. The literature review will be organized according to theme. Tech-savvy but critical scholars. Probably trained in STS (Latour, Law, Benjamin etc). I need to write this literature review. Don’t write it for me. Instead, be my dialectical guide. Using criteria, structural principle and audience, help me develop the synopsis into an ‘A’ grade paper! </dialectic_guide

Re-cap on course purpose

Dual: - ERAM - focus on mechanics, technical detail of the literature review - But also examine how AI is being worked into practices of scholarship - and to be attentive and crtical towards that - Future is complex, challenging - “cyber-social” – with mixed effects and opportunities - Need for critical AI literacies - stay vigilant!

EPOL 590 AI and Academic Literature

Fall 2026 Term B · Section AIL · CRN 73886 · 4 credit hours

Instructor working draft — not ready for release. The section details below are verified. The final literature review is due Tuesday, December 15, 2026, at 11:59 PM Central. Other assignment dates and specifications remain proposals pending instructor review. Items marked [TO CONFIRM] must be completed before publication.

Course information

Course site: https://canvas.illinois.edu/courses/75598

  • Instructor: Professor Liam Magee, Education Policy, Organization and Leadership, College of Education. Email: lmagee@illinois.edu.
  • Meetings: online, Mondays 5:00–7:50 PM Central Time (America/Chicago).
  • Seminar dates: October 19 and 26; November 2, 9, 16, and 30; December 7.
  • Term: October 19–December 9. No seminar or new required submission during fall break, November 21–29.
  • Meeting access: [TO CONFIRM] Zoom link and access instructions.
  • Office hours: meetings by appointment; email lmagee@illinois.edu to arrange a time.

Official registration details: Illinois Course Explorer. The registered course is EPOL 590; older teaching materials use ERAM 590.

Course description

How do we conduct scholarly research in an era of generative AI? This graduate course combines the fundamentals of a rigorous literature review with a critical examination of AI-assisted scholarship. You will develop a research question, locate and organize relevant literature, read closely and across a field, and turn that work into a persuasive scholarly argument.

The practical work and the critical questions belong together. AI can produce a summary, propose a conceptual map, or suggest a gap. We will ask how those outputs were made, whose knowledge they privilege, what they miss, and what responsibility remains with the researcher.

The course is cumulative: you develop and revise one review through the staged assignments. It may support a dissertation, journal article, or another research project; an exploratory review is also welcome.

Learning objectives

  1. Develop and revise a significant, feasible research question through engagement with literature.
  2. Design a transparent approach to finding, selecting, and organizing sources.
  3. Use close reading and mapping to analyze relationships, disagreements, omissions, and possible contributions.
  4. Write a coherent synthesis for a scholarly audience, with effective structure, citation, and signposting.
  5. Explain how positionality and knowledge communities shape research questions and interpretation.
  6. Evaluate AI-assisted research outputs, verify sources, and account for how AI influenced the work.

Teaching sequence and proposed milestones

Seminars and proposed assessment dates in 2026
Seminar Focus Proposed submission Weight
October 19 Research questions Topic and question — October 23 10%
October 26 Review design and article anatomy Review design — October 30 10%
November 2 AI-assisted reading and mapping Conceptual map — November 6 10%
November 9 Difficult texts and scholarly voice Writing sample — November 13 10%
November 16 Structure and signposting Structured draft — November 20 10%
November 21–29 Fall break No new required submission —
November 30 Reflexivity and AI use AI-use statement and commentary — December 4 10%
December 7 Final review workshop Final review — December 15 40%

All proposed due times are 11:59 PM Central. The final literature review is due Tuesday, December 15, 2026, at 11:59 PM Central. This course deadline is confirmed. The Course Summary below reflects the dates entered in Canvas.

Assessment and submission

The six staged assignments together contribute 60% of the course grade, with equal weighting of 10% each. The final literature review contributes 40%. Each Canvas assignment is marked out of 100. Peer workshops support revision and have no separate grade weight.

Use the corresponding Canvas assignment for instructions and submission. File upload is the proposed submission method. Draft task lengths and source expectations are recorded there for instructor review. The final literature review is 1,500–2,000 words.

Assessment emphasizes the significance and feasibility of the question, source relevance and traceability, interpretation and synthesis, organization and scholarly voice, reflexivity and transparent AI use, and revision in response to evidence and feedback. [TO CONFIRM] Detailed rubrics, grade boundaries, and rounding.

Preparation and readings

Bring an article, an uncertain interpretation, a draft section, or a search problem to each workshop. Keep a concise record of your question, search decisions, source notes, maps, revisions, feedback, and consequential AI use. [TO CONFIRM] Workload and additional guided online activities for the compressed four-credit course.

No book purchase is proposed. A suggested starting resource is Purdue OWL Writing a Literature Review, together with articles from your own field. Weber, Spivak, and the sociology-of-knowledge readings remain candidates; [TO CONFIRM] final selections, editions, excerpts, and accessible access. Imported lecture pages and 2025 slides require review before release.

AI use and access

AI is an object of study and a possible research tool. Verify citations against actual sources, distinguish an author's claim from your interpretation and an AI suggestion, and describe consequential AI assistance in submissions. Do not present fabricated references, unverified quotations, or analysis you cannot explain as established scholarship.

No paid AI subscription is required by this draft. Proposed alternative: analyze instructor-supplied prompts and outputs when a live tool is unavailable. Do not upload confidential, identifiable, or restricted material to an AI service. [TO CONFIRM] Final permitted tools, activity alternatives, and course AI policy.

Course arrangements and support

Attendance and peer work: participate in the seminars and workshops. Contact me if you need an equivalent way to engage. An anonymized extract or instructor-mediated exchange is proposed as an alternative to peer sharing. [TO CONFIRM] Attendance requirements and workshop arrangements.

Late work and feedback: contact me when a deadline creates difficulty so we can plan how the cumulative work will continue. [TO CONFIRM] Extension and late-work rules, final cutoff, and feedback turnaround. No automatic late penalty is established by this draft.

Accessibility: contact me privately about barriers to participation or materials. Disability Resources and Educational Services coordinates disability-related academic accommodations. Share a Letter of Accommodations through the University's arrangements so we can discuss implementation; diagnostic information need not be shared with the class or instructor. [TO CONFIRM] Final College wording and accessibility review of materials.

Academic integrity: the University Student Code applies. Attribute others' words and ideas, use only permitted assistance, and do not invent evidence or citations. Ask when AI permissions are unclear. Suspected violations follow University procedures.

Recording and sharing: [TO CONFIRM] Whether seminars are recorded, access, consent, and retention arrangements. Course recordings and peer documents must not be assumed available for sharing outside the class.

Student support: Illinois Counseling Center. [TO CONFIRM] Remaining current University and College syllabus statements.
